notes:
I found sources for most verses. Some gaps: I read no Lutheran or Orthodox page, no explicitly Methodist or Wesleyan page, and no Bible Odyssey article. The NET Bible result showed only its translation, not its notes. Nothing turned up on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Where a page gives a commentator's tradition I include it; otherwise I leave the label off.

**Main sources**
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-66/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-66.html
- **Bible Hub commentary pages, verse 24:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-24.htm (Ellicott, Benson, Matthew Henry, Barnes)

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** God rules from heaven, so no earthly temple can hold him. Guzik notes that Stephen quotes vv. 1–2 in Acts 7. (Enduring Word)
- **What the temple is:** Ellicott says the verse states that God doesn't live in temples made by hands. He adds that this is compatible with deep respect for the temple, as Solomon, Jesus and Stephen all showed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** God fills all things and can't be confined to any place. The prophet's target is worshippers who are pleased with themselves and pretend to serve God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/66-1.html
- **Which temple is meant? The views differ:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says God is rebuking ungodly exiles planning to rebuild the temple. They were unworthy to build it, which is why he refused. (Pulpit page)
  - Barnes reports several older views. Lowth and Vitringa thought of Herod's temple, Grotius of the Maccabean period, and the Jewish commentator Abarbanel of the future redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-1.htm
  - Chuck Smith applies it to a future temple probably built under the Antichrist's covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/66-1.html
- **Older scholarly comment:** Ellicott says we can only guess at the historical setting. Critics have suggested a restored post-exile temple or one built in exile. He notes Cheyne's parallel from an Egyptian Nile hymn: no building can contain God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says God wants a humble, contrite heart that trembles at his word, not something we build. Quoting Motyer, he says "contrite" literally means "lamed": aware of sin's damage. (Enduring Word)
- **Pulpit:** Translates "all these things came into being" at God's word. God made everyone but doesn't regard everyone equally. (Pulpit page)

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says a sacrifice offered without the right spirit pleases God no more than murder or offering an unclean dog. Here the sacrifices are planned, not yet offered, and God rejects them in advance. (Pulpit page)
  - Guzik: their ritual added to their sin instead of removing it. (Enduring Word)
- **Pointing to Christ:** Matthew Henry, quoted on the Bible Hub page, says anything put in place of Christ's priesthood and atonement is hateful to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-1.htm

**v. 4**
- **"Their punishment" may also be read "their delusions":** God sends delusion on those who chose their own ways (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:11). (Pulpit page)
- **Guzik:** Links this to the Great Tribulation. The cure is to answer when God calls. (Enduring Word)

**v. 5**
- **Pulpit:** The faithful are being addressed. "Cast out" later came to mean formal excommunication, but here it just means rejecting their fellowship. The brothers' words are sarcasm: "May the prophecies come true." (Pulpit page)
- **Guzik:** Describes how empty religion hates, rejects and mocks genuine faith in God's name, but will be put to shame. (Enduring Word)

**v. 6**
- **Pulpit:** The prophet sees Jerusalem and the temple suddenly rebuilt. The restored state later did subdue some of its old enemies. (Pulpit page)
- **Guzik:** Shame comes "at the end of days, if not before." (Enduring Word)

**v. 7**
- **Traditional reading:** Zion gives birth to a whole nation at once, without labour pains. The Pulpit Commentary takes this as the returned exiles occupying Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/66-7.htm
- **Guzik:** Victory comes easily to Jerusalem. (Enduring Word)
- **Catholic reading:** Catholic Answers uses this verse, together with early Christian writers and church teaching, as evidence that Mary gave birth to Jesus without pain. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/evidence-for-marys-painless-childbirth

**v. 8**
- **Pulpit:** A land is reborn, not only a people: Judaea as well as the Jews. (Pulpit page)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** His sermon "Travailing for Souls" draws from this verse that spiritual birth requires travail first. https://biblehub.com/study/isaiah/66-21.htm

**v. 9**
- **Pulpit:** Having prepared everything for his people's restoration, God won't stop at the last moment. (Pulpit page)

**vv. 10–11**
- **Pulpit:** Everyone who loves Jerusalem, Jews and foreigners alike, is called to rejoice. She will feed them like a mother, with the "milk of the Word" (1 Peter 2:2). (Pulpit page)
- **Guzik:** Includes Spurgeon's remark that if the world calls us fanatics, we are nearing the zeal the Lord deserves. (Enduring Word)

**v. 12**
- **Pulpit:** Peace is "directed" to her as farmers direct water channels. The nations' wealth overflows her the way Assyria once flooded Israel, but now to bless her, not destroy her. (Pulpit page)
- **Disputed detail:** The Pulpit Commentary says Jerusalem, not the Gentile world, carries the children. It notes that Delitzsch and Cheyne disagree. (Pulpit page)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic list):** Applies the verse to Jerusalem's peace when the Messiah returns. (Enduring Word)

**v. 13**
- **Guzik:** Quotes Spurgeon: God compares himself to a father when he speaks of pity, but to a mother when he speaks of comfort. (Enduring Word)
- **Pulpit:** The singular "as a man" pictures Israel as grown up, now comforted by God himself. (Pulpit page)

**v. 14**
- **Pulpit:** Bones once wasted by trouble will flourish again. God's hand is seen both in mercy and in anger, which leads into vv. 15–18. (Pulpit page)

**v. 15**
- **Pulpit:** Fire regularly accompanies God's appearing (Sinai, Elijah). It links this to the fire at Christ's second coming (2 Thessalonians 1:8; 2 Peter 3). Following Cheyne, it takes the chariots as God's forces. (Pulpit page)
- **Guzik:** Applies it to the Messiah's return. (Enduring Word)

**v. 16**
- **Pulpit:** Following Delitzsch, fire stands for natural disasters and the sword for disasters of history. "Plead with" should be read "judge." (Pulpit page)
- **Benson:** Also applies the verse to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-24.htm

**v. 17**
- **Pulpit:** "One in the center" is either a cult leader (Gesenius, Delitzsch) or an idol whose name worshippers avoided saying (Grotius, Cheyne). "Rats" is probably the jerboa. (Pulpit page)
- **Guzik:** The Messiah will see through empty religion. (Enduring Word)

**v. 18**
- **Pulpit:** The Hebrew is missing a verb. "I know" is supported by the Targum, the Syriac and others. Cheyne supplies "I will punish." The Pulpit Commentary rejects using "nations and tongues" as proof of late authorship, since the pairing already appears in Genesis 10. (Pulpit page)

**v. 19**
- **The "sign":**
  - Kay suggests Christ's resurrection, while Cheyne sees only an undefined mysterious event. (Pulpit page)
  - Guzik quotes Bultema: it is the "sign of the Son of man" (Matthew 24:30). (Enduring Word)
- **The text:** "Pul" (KJV) is almost certainly a mistake for "Put" (an African people). The survivors are the faithful Jewish remnant, not surviving enemies. (Pulpit page)
- **Where Protestants differ on fulfilment:**
  - Guzik sees partial fulfilment in church missions. Its final fulfilment may be the 144,000 of Revelation or Jewish evangelists in the millennium. (Enduring Word)
  - Calvin sees here the renewal and worldwide spread of the Church. https://www.ccel.org/study/Isaiah_66:1-3?commentary=2&tab=commentary&version=nrsv

**v. 20**
- **Pulpit:** Converted Gentiles bring scattered Jews to Christ. The comparison with Israel's offerings assumes the temple was still standing. (Pulpit page)
- **Matthew Henry:** Takes the details as figures of the many means God uses to bring his chosen people to Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-24.htm
- **Guzik:** Partly fulfilled in Israel's modern regathering, finally fulfilled in the millennium. (Enduring Word)
- **Pulpit sermon notes:** The proper "victory" over a brother is to bring him to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/isaiah/66.htm

**v. 21: who are "them"?**
- **Restored Israelites:** Ellicott leans this way: all Israel would be eligible for the priesthood, an idea later widened to all of faith. A. B. Davidson also thinks this more likely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-21.htm
- **Converted Gentiles, fulfilled in the church:**
  - Benson, Barnes, Gill and Delitzsch read it this way.
  - The Bible Hub sermon notes say it was never fulfilled literally but is fulfilled in Christ's kingdom.
  - The Pulpit Commentary adds Gentile members to an existing priesthood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-21.htm
  - Gill reads it figuratively and spiritually, as ministers in Gospel churches. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/gnt/isaiah/66-21.html
  - Guzik quotes Motyer: Gentiles are brought in on equal terms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-66/
  - Matthew Henry: some, not all, are made ministers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_066.cfm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** God takes from Jews and Gentiles a people he brings near and uses for his purposes. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-new-order-of-priests-and-levites
- **Literal millennium view:** One Bible Hub study note has Gentile priests serving alongside Israelite priests in Christ's millennial reign. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/66-21.htm

**v. 22**
- **Pulpit:** The verse is usually read as a special privilege for Jews. The Pulpit Commentary prefers to read it as "a seed of true believers" always remaining, since Paul treats such privileges as abolished (Colossians 3:11). (Pulpit page)

**v. 23**
- **Pulpit:** The phrase means continuous worship, not that New Moon and Sabbath rules continue. Quoting Pusey, all mankind can't worship in one place, which points to worship like that in John 4:21. (Pulpit page)

**v. 24**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Jesus applies this verse to hell in Mark 9. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/isaiah/66-24.html
  - Matthew Henry and Barnes read it as the final suffering of the wicked. Barnes ties the imagery to the valley of Hinnom (Gehenna). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-24.htm
- **Two layers:** Benson sees the Roman destruction first, then mainly punishment in the world to come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-24.htm
- **Constable:** Includes those killed at Armageddon and those condemned forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/66-24.html
- **Ellicott, more cautious:**
  - Read strictly, the verse describes enemies destroyed on earth, not souls after death.
  - The undying worm hints at more, and the verse became the starting point for later Jewish teaching on Gehenna.
  - Whether bodies are tormented or consumed is still an open question for him.
  - The verse does tend to rule out suffering that purifies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-24.htm
- **Annihilationism (a debated evangelical view):**
  - Got Questions reports the argument of those who hold "conditional immortality": the verse speaks of corpses, and elsewhere unquenchable fire consumes completely. https://www.gotquestions.org/conditional-immortality.html
  - Against this, the Pulpit Commentary says the images imply everlasting continuance and calls both universalism and annihilationism "heresies." (Pulpit page)
  - Don Stewart also uses the verse against annihilation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/faq/don_stewart/don_stewart_177.cfm
- **Synagogue custom:** When this chapter was read, the last verse but one was repeated afterwards so that mercy came last. The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott both mention this. (Pulpit page; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/66-24.htm)
